title: How Music Sampling Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain music sampling: what a sample is, the business and legal history behind it, and the cultural debate over credit and compensation. They cover Bridgeport Music and its "sample troll" lawsuits (including against Jay Z over Madonna's "Justify My Love"), and classic breaks like James Brown's "Funky Drummer" (drummer Clyde Stubblefield) and the Winstons' "Amen, Brother" (drummer Gregory Sylvester Coleman). They trace sampling's origins from musique concrète (Pierre Schaeffer, Pierre Henry, Pierre Henry/Pierre Schaeffer) and tape splicing, the Mellotron, Dickie Goodman and Bill Buchanan's "Flying Saucer" break-in records, James Tenney's "Collage #1 (Blue Suede)", DJ Kool Herc, Grandmaster Flash, Marley Marl, and the Beastie Boys' "Paul's Boutique". They recount the 1991 Gilbert O'Sullivan "Alone Again (Naturally)" case against Biz Markie and Warner Brothers that shifted sampling from art to business, the shift to buyouts and royalty rates, Vanilla Ice and Queen's "Under Pressure", the Newton v. Diamond case over a three-note flute sample, Danger Mouse's "The Grey Album", cover song rules, and fair use. The episode ends with listener mail from Tom about his family's run-ins with suspicion of being spies in France and a Nazi-era story about his great-great aunt, Sister Marie.

entities.name: Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five

segments.title: Opening banter and sampling intro
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter and a sponsor plug, then introduce Bridgeport Music and its lawsuits against samplers, including Jay Z over Madonna's 'Justify My Love', and the idea of 'sample trolls'.

segments.title: What a sample is and classic breaks
segments.summary: They define sampling as taking a piece of an existing recording and looping it into something new. They discuss James Brown's 'Funky Drummer' and drummer Clyde Stubblefield, and the Winstons' 'Amen, Brother' break and Gregory Sylvester Coleman, which gave rise to jungle.

segments.title: Sampling examples in hits and rock
segments.summary: Ladies Love Cool James is cited as built on the Funky Drummer and Sly and the Family Stone backing vocals. They also cite samples of films and speeches in Living Color, Guns N' Roses, and Metallica.

segments.title: Early sampling: Mellotron and musique concrète
segments.summary: The Mellotron is described as an early sampling keyboard, used on the Beatles' 'Strawberry Fields Forever'. Before that, tape splicing was used, and Pierre Schaeffer and Pierre Henry created musique concrète.

segments.title: Flying Saucer records and experimental collage
segments.summary: James Tenney's 'Collage #1 (Blue Suede)' is discussed as a deconstruction of Elvis Presley. Dickie Goodman and Bill Buchanan's 'Flying Saucer' (1956) mashed up rock hits with fake news reports, and the hosts recall similar radio mash-ups later.

segments.title: Turntable sampling and hip hop pioneers
segments.summary: They discuss DJ Kool Herc's early turntable breakbeats, Grandmaster Flash's scratching and 'Freedom', which sampled 'Get Up and Dance', and Marley Marl as a house producer for the Juice Crew.

segments.title: Beastie Boys, Public Enemy, and the shift to clearance
segments.summary: The Beastie Boys' 'Paul's Boutique' and Public Enemy built songs from dozens of samples. The hosts note that clearance costs made such dense sampling harder, and that artists now often use a single loop.

segments.title: Gilbert O'Sullivan case and sampling becomes business
segments.summary: Biz Markie's use of 'Alone Again (Naturally)' led to a ruling against Warner Brothers. The judge's remarks on possible criminal prosecution shut down open sampling, and it became a business with buyouts and royalties.

segments.title: Costs, Vanilla Ice, Newton v. Diamond, and other cases
segments.summary: They discuss royalty rates and the split between composition and recording rights. Vanilla Ice's use of Queen's 'Under Pressure' is discussed, along with MC Hammer and the Newton v. Diamond case over a three-note flute sample, which the Beastie Boys won.
topics: Led Zeppelin When the Levee Breaks

segments.title: Danger Mouse, cover songs, and fair use
segments.summary: The Grey Album by Danger Mouse, a mash-up of the Beatles' White Album and Jay Z's Black Album, was shut down by EMI. The hosts discuss cover song rules and explain fair use as the reason they can play clips.

segments.title: Outro
segments.summary: Sign-off with the show's contact information and sponsor reminders.
